title: The Odd Women: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: The New Woman and Her Convictions: Opening Rhoda's World

utterances.text: Welcome to The Odd Women Unpacked — a close, spirited reading of George Gissing's remarkable 1893 novel.
Each episode, we work through the novel chapter by chapter, bringing together literary, historical, and readerly perspectives.
The Odd Women is one of the most searching novels about women's lives, work, and freedom ever written in English.

It centres on the Madden sisters — daughters of a country doctor left suddenly without means — and on Rhoda Nunn and Mary Barfoot, two women who have built something extraordinary in their refusal to be quietly ruined.
Today we open with the world Gissing constructs for Rhoda — her convictions, her contradictions, and what it means to call her a New Woman.
Let me introduce our three guests, each of whom brings something indispensable to this conversation.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose obsession is how great fiction is built — the architecture of the sentence, the weight of a single image.
She is exactly who you want in the room when a passage repays close attention — which, in Gissing, is most of the time.
Prof. James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions literature depicts — the law, the workplace, the marriage contract.
He has a gift for making the world behind the page feel urgent and real — and occasionally, quietly furious about it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read The Odd Women as a teenager and has never quite let go of it.
She attends to the experience of reading — the moments that make you stop, re-read, and feel something shift.
Let's begin where Gissing begins — with the world his women inhabit, and with the extraordinary figure of Rhoda Nunn at its centre.
What strikes me immediately about how Gissing opens this novel is the brutality of the prologue — if we can call it that.
We get the Madden family in what feels like a pastoral sketch — Dr. Madden, his daughters, a summer evening of apparent security — and then Gissing simply removes the floor.
The father dies, the money is gone, and the daughters must face a world that has no interest in their refinement or their virtue.
It's a structural choice that announces the novel's argument before a single word of it has been made — that genteel female poverty is not a misfortune, it is a system.
And against that system, Gissing sets Rhoda Nunn — who enters the novel as a young girl in the Madden household and returns, years later, as someone who has decided what she thinks.
The distance between those two appearances is the novel's spine.
Eleanor's point about the system is the key to reading the novel historically.
In 1893 — the year of publication — there were something in the region of half a million more women than men in England.
The demographic reality was that a great many women would never marry — not by choice, but by arithmetic.
And a woman without a husband, without a profession, without capital, was — to use a blunt word — destitute.
Gissing's title is drawn from that surplus — these are the women left over, uncounted in the social arithmetic.
What Mary Barfoot and Rhoda Nunn are doing, in their typewriting school, is not charity — it is a strategic intervention in that arithmetic.
They are trying to make women economically legible in a world that has refused to see them.
I want to come back to Rhoda herself, because I think she is one of the most extraordinary characters in Victorian fiction — and also one of the most uncomfortable to spend time with.
When we first meet the adult Rhoda through Monica Madden's eyes, she is striking, purposeful, and faintly alarming.
Gissing gives her a face that is not conventionally pretty but arresting — there's an energy in her that the novel keeps describing as something almost combative.
And her convictions — her belief that women must be self-reliant, that marriage as presently constituted is a trap — are held with a fervour that makes other characters uneasy.
Gissing gives her a line that I have never forgotten, about the odd women — about the surplus women who, in his framing, might become the vanguard of a new order rather than its victims.
She speaks of making women who are not constrained by the old feminine ideal — and she means it absolutely.
The question the novel asks — and never quite resolves — is whether Rhoda's certainty is wisdom or another kind of cage.
Caroline's word — cage — is the right one, and I think Gissing earns it through a very deliberate narrative strategy.
He never tells us directly that Rhoda is wrong — he is too intelligent and too sympathetic a writer for that.

But he places her convictions under pressure through the plot — specifically through the arrival of Everard Barfoot and what happens to Rhoda when she is looked at and found interesting by a man of genuine intelligence.
The irony Gissing is constructing — very quietly, very patiently — is that Rhoda's theory of women's freedom may not have accounted for Rhoda's own desires.
That is a devastating thing to do to a character, but it is also an act of profound respect — he takes her seriously enough to test her.
There's a legal and economic dimension to Everard's arrival that I think sharpens what Eleanor is describing.
Everard Barfoot is a man of independent means — he has capital, he has leisure, he has the freedom to philosophise about free unions because he can afford the consequences.
Rhoda has none of that backstop.
When she debates the question of marriage with him, she is debating it from a position of genuine economic precarity — and he is not.
Gissing understood — as few of his contemporaries did — that freedom of the mind is much harder to achieve when freedom of circumstance is withheld.
What moves me most, reading the opening sections again, is the tenderness Gissing shows for the Madden sisters alongside his rather steelier portrait of Rhoda.
Alice and Virginia Madden are not equipped for what life has brought them — and Gissing never condescends to them for that.
They are casualties of an education that trained them only for dependency — and that critique is as sharp now as it was in 1893.
Monica is the youngest, still with some brightness in her, and her predicament — the shop counter, the grinding hours, the respectable poverty — is almost unbearable.
These are the women Rhoda is trying to save — and it matters that Gissing makes us feel the weight of their actual lives before he gives us Rhoda's programme.
That distinction — between the women who need saving and the woman with the theory of how to save them — feels like the engine of the whole novel.
And it opens directly onto the questions we'll take up next — about class, about the marriage market, and about what Gissing really thought society owed its women.

segments.title: A Society in Flux: Class, Gender, and the Marriage Question

utterances.text: We've been exploring Rhoda Nunn's fierce intellectual convictions and the world she's built at the typewriting school.
But those convictions don't exist in a vacuum — they're a direct response to a society whose institutions are themselves cracking under pressure.

So let's widen the frame now and look at the broader social landscape Gissing is mapping: class anxiety, the marriage market, and what it actually meant for a woman to be financially dependent in 1893.
It's worth pausing on what Gissing means by the title itself — the odd women.
He's drawing on the demographic reality of mid-Victorian England, where census data consistently showed a surplus of women — hundreds of thousands who would simply never find husbands.
These women were statistically odd, in the sense of being the remainder — left over once the pairing was done.
And the novel opens by confronting that arithmetic brutally, through the Madden sisters.
Their father has given them accomplishments — a little piano, a little French — but no practical training whatsoever, because he assumed marriage would take care of everything.
His death is catastrophic not just emotionally but economically, and Gissing makes absolutely certain we feel the causal chain.
And the way Gissing handles that opening is structurally very bold.
He compresses years of decline into the first chapter — almost like a time-lapse of a family's ruin.
Each sister's fate is sketched with this quiet, clinical precision — a marriage here, a death there, a gradual slide into poverty.
It reads almost like a ledger.
And I think that ledger quality is intentional — Gissing wants us to understand that women's lives in this period were subject to exactly this kind of cold economic accounting.
The novel's form is doing ideological work from the very first page.
What breaks my heart every time I reread that opening is Alice Madden specifically.
She's the eldest, she's diligent, she tries so hard — and the world simply has no place for her trying.
Gissing gives her this painful religiosity that she retreats into, and it reads as the only consolation available to a woman with no economic recourse.
Mary Barfoot says something quite devastating about women like the Maddens at one point — she talks about them being trained for a function that may never be required of them.
"Trained for a function which, in many cases, can never be discharged."
That word — discharged — carries such a weight of futility and waste.
Mary Barfoot is really the novel's great explainer of systems, isn't she.
She understands that the problem isn't individual misfortune — it's structural.

And the historical reality she's describing is precise: middle-class women had almost no access to education that led to employment, and almost no employment that was socially acceptable if they did manage to get educated.
The typewriting school isn't a fantasy — it's a direct response to the actual opening up of clerical work to women in the 1880s and 1890s.
Gissing knew that world.
He was writing from within it, not at a comfortable distance.
And yet for all Barfoot and Rhoda's clarity about the system, the novel keeps testing their convictions through the marriage question itself.
Everard Barfoot arrives and rather complicates the programme.
Everard is such a technically interesting creation precisely because Gissing refuses to make him simply a villain or simply a hero.
He's genuinely attracted to Rhoda's intelligence.
He claims to want a free union, a companionship of equals — and on the surface those are progressive positions.
But Gissing keeps showing us the gap between what Everard says and the possession instinct that runs just below his liberal surface.
He wants Rhoda to choose him freely — but on his terms, in his frame, at his timing.

There's a very sharp moment when he essentially proposes a secret arrangement, and Rhoda recognises that even this supposedly radical offer is still asking her to sacrifice her public credibility — her usefulness to other women.
That confrontation is one of the most electrically written scenes in the novel, I think.
Because Rhoda is genuinely tempted.
Gissing doesn't let her be simply a programme.
She feels desire — intellectual and physical — and that vulnerability is what makes the scene agonising.
She asks herself at one point what it would mean to give up the work — and Gissing renders her answer as something discovered rather than preached.
"It would be the defeat of a cause."
That's not a slogan — that's a woman working out what she actually believes under pressure.
What I find historically fascinating is Everard's proposal of a free union specifically — without legal marriage.
That position was very much in the air in the 1880s and early 1890s — the question of whether the marriage contract itself was a form of property law applied to women.
The Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 had changed some of that, but the social stigma of any irregular arrangement fell almost entirely on the woman.
So when Everard offers Rhoda freedom from the institution, he's actually offering her the full weight of public shame with none of the legal protections.
That's not liberation — that's a rather elegant trap.
Exactly — and Gissing encodes that trap in the language Everard uses.
He speaks of equality and freedom but the grammar of his proposals is consistently that of a man who expects to be heard.
There's a recurring pattern where he poses questions that are really demands with a question mark attached.
And he is convinced — with what Gissing calls almost a kind of intellectual vanity — that Rhoda will ultimately come to his position.
The craft achievement is that we can see exactly why Rhoda finds him compelling, even as we see through him.
And the novel places all of this against the much starker story of Monica Madden, who does choose the conventional path — and finds it a different kind of trap entirely.
Monica and her husband Widdowson — that's exactly where we're heading next.

segments.title: The Trap of Domesticity: Monica's Descent and Widdowson's Obsession

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Gissing maps the larger social pressures bearing down on women in the 1890s.
Now I want to narrow the lens — to Monica Madden, and to the marriage that was supposed to save her.
Monica is the character who breaks your heart most cleanly in this novel, I think.
She begins as someone genuinely alive to possibility — she's young, she's restless, she's working in a draper's shop and finding it suffocating.
And Gissing makes you feel the texture of that suffocation — the long hours, the cramped dormitory, the relentless smallness of it.
So when Edmund Widdowson appears with his income and his respectability, you understand exactly why she says yes.
It isn't love, and Gissing doesn't pretend it is.
It's a calculation made by someone who has run out of better options — and that is the trap closing.
And legally, socially, once that trap closes, it locks from the outside.
What Gissing renders so precisely is the Victorian doctrine of coverture — the legal fiction that husband and wife are one person, and that person is the husband.
Monica's earnings, her movements, her very right to be in public space — all of it becomes subject to Widdowson's authority the moment they marry.
He isn't portrayed as a monster, which is what makes him so disturbing.
He genuinely believes that keeping Monica confined to the home is an act of love and protection.
That gap between his self-perception and the reality of what he does to her — that is Gissing's sharpest critique of the institution.
Gissing actually gives us Widdowson's interiority quite generously, which is a brave structural choice.
There are passages where we're entirely inside Widdowson's perspective — his jealousy, his bewilderment, his sense of righteous grievance.
And Gissing doesn't editorialize heavily — he lets the reader do the moral work.
Widdowson's surveillance of Monica — following her through London, timing her movements — is rendered in his own terms as vigilance, as husbandly duty.
The narrative lets that self-justification stand, and then shows us what it looks like from Monica's side.
The technique is almost cinematic — cutting between perspectives to create an irony the characters themselves cannot see.
That moment when Widdowson follows Monica to Battersea Park — it's almost unbearable to read.
Because Monica is doing nothing wrong — she's simply out, simply breathing air that isn't the air of her own drawing room.
And Gissing writes Widdowson's suspicion as a kind of madness — methodical, self-reinforcing, impervious to evidence.
There's a line where he reflects that a wife's place is beside her husband, that any wish for independence is in itself a form of disloyalty.
"A wife's thought should be her husband's thought; a wife's pleasure, her husband's pleasure."
The repetition there is doing everything — it's an incantation, and he believes it absolutely.
That sense of total possession isn't aberrant for its time — it's almost the mainstream ideal.
Conduct manuals of the 1880s and 1890s said almost exactly what Widdowson believes — that the well-ordered home required a wife's complete devotion.
What Gissing is showing us is that Widdowson is not a villain — he's a symptom.
And that indictment is more devastating than any villain could produce.
There's a scene I keep returning to, where Monica attempts to articulate her unhappiness to Widdowson.
She reaches for the words — and Gissing shows us the reaching, the groping toward a language she doesn't quite possess.
Because the vocabulary for a wife's legitimate grievance within marriage barely exists in her world.
Rhoda Nunn has that vocabulary — she's developed it through reading, through Barfoot, through conscious rebellion.
But Monica was never given those intellectual tools, and that makes her vulnerability structural, not personal.
And then Everard Barfoot enters Monica's orbit — and it feels, for a moment, like oxygen.
He's witty, he treats her as an intelligent person, he isn't Widdowson.
But Gissing doesn't let us be comforted by that — Barfoot is charming in the way of men who can afford to be charming.
He's pursuing Monica as much for the intellectual game of it as for any genuine feeling.
And Monica, desperate for any acknowledgment of her inner life, mistakes the attention for something it is not.
The geography of their meetings is telling — they meet in public spaces because those are the only spaces Monica can access unsupervised.
The park, the street, the railway — these become sites of a kind of illicit freedom for her.
And of course those same public spaces are where Widdowson's surveillance is most ferocious.
Gissing understands that for women of Monica's class, public space was itself contested territory — simultaneously the only escape and the site of maximum danger.
What strikes me as a formally daring choice is how Gissing handles the novel's end for Monica.
She dies — in childbirth, essentially of despair — and the novel doesn't dramatize her death as tragedy in the grand operatic sense.
It's quiet, almost reported, as if the system that killed her is so routine it barely requires ceremony.
That flatness is the point — Monica's life is swallowed by the institution of marriage and what remains is an administrative fact.
Gissing refuses her the dignity of a dramatic exit, and I think that refusal is itself a form of rage.
I find Monica's final weeks — the estrangement, the failed reconciliation, the slow physical collapse — almost impossible to read quickly.
Gissing keeps returning Widdowson to her bedside, still not quite understanding what he has done.
He grieves, but his grief is for the wife he imagined — not the woman she actually was.
There's something unspeakably sad about that — that Monica dies still unseen by the man who believed he loved her most.
What you're describing — that gap between love as possession and love as genuine recognition — seems to be one of Gissing's great, repeated preoccupations in this novel.
And it raises a question about how the narrative voice itself manages that material — with what degree of irony, what kind of distance.
That's exactly where we're headed next — to Gissing's narrative voice, and the peculiar tonal balance he strikes between anger and comedy.

segments.title: Irony and Unease: Gissing's Narrative Voice and Comic Distance

utterances.text: We've been tracking Monica's entrapment — the slow suffocation of her marriage to Widdowson.
But Gissing doesn't deliver that story in anguished, melodramatic prose — and that's what makes it so unsettling.
His narrative voice maintains a cool, ironic distance — even as the characters around him are falling apart.
So let's talk about Gissing as a stylist — that voice, that comic distance, and what it costs the reader emotionally.
The thing that strikes me every time I return to this novel is that Gissing writes irony as a form of restraint — not detachment.
There's a crucial difference, and it's the difference between a novelist who doesn't care and one who cares almost too much.
Think about how he handles Everard Barfoot — that rakish intellectual who circles around Rhoda Nunn.
Gissing gives Barfoot wonderfully persuasive arguments for free unions, for women's emancipation — and then quietly lets us watch him deploy those arguments as seduction.
The irony is structural — it's built into the gap between what characters say and what they want.
And Gissing never annotates it for us — he just holds the frame steady and trusts us to see.
That structural irony has a social dimension too, and I think it's where Gissing is most uncomfortably precise.
He's writing about a particular stratum of English society — the genteel poor, the educated but unprovided-for — with the intimacy of someone who has lived it.
And the comedy, such as it is, comes from the gulf between the pretensions of respectability and the grinding material reality underneath.
There's a moment where the narrator describes Widdowson's domestic arrangements — his routines, his little proprieties — with a precision that reads almost like a naturalist cataloguing a specimen.
The comedy and the horror are inseparable — because the specimen doesn't know it's being observed.
James's word — 'horror' — is exactly right, and I want to hold onto that for a moment.
Because when you actually read Gissing's prose aloud, you feel the comedy and the dread arriving simultaneously — in the same sentence, sometimes the same clause.
His narrator has this quality of seeming to report neutrally — and yet every word is chosen with a kind of cold surgical precision.

There's a line I keep coming back to — from the passages where Rhoda reflects on the women she's trying to help — where Gissing writes something to the effect that their lives had 'the monotony of hopeless effort.'
'The monotony of hopeless effort.'
Three words — and the whole tragic comedy of the novel is compressed into them.
What Caroline is pointing to is something I'd call Gissing's tonal tightrope.
He is writing comedy of manners — and yet every laugh curdles slightly as it leaves your mouth.
Think about the scenes involving Mr. Micklethwaite — Barfoot's old friend who finally marries his long-betrothed after decades of waiting.
On paper that's warm and comic — fidelity rewarded, love enduring poverty.
But Gissing frames it so that the very happiness of Micklethwaite and his wife reads as an indictment of a society that made them wait so long for so little.
The sentiment is real — and so is the critique embedded inside it.
The Micklethwaite episode is interesting because it's one of the few places where Gissing permits himself something approaching sentimentality — and he immediately quarantines it.
He places it well away from the main action — it's almost a parenthetical in the novel's emotional economy.
As if Gissing allows himself one warm room in the house — and then locks the door.
The dominant register elsewhere is that measured, slightly weary irony — which is the irony of a man who has looked at his society and found it wanting, but who will not shout.
He whispers, very carefully, with excellent diction.
That's such a precise way to put it — 'whispers with excellent diction.'
And it connects to what makes the Rhoda and Barfoot courtship so uncomfortable to read.
Rhoda is the novel's most formidable intelligence — she has theories, principles, a mission.
And Gissing's narrator watches, almost clinically, as those principles are tested by desire.
He doesn't mock her — that's the key thing.
He records the conflict with something I can only describe as compassionate precision — which is far more devastating than mockery would be.
'Compassionate precision' — I'm going to borrow that phrase, Caroline.
It explains why the novel's comedy never tips into farce and its tragedy never tips into melodrama.
Gissing is always at this exact fulcrum — and it's an extraordinarily difficult place to write from.
Think about the title itself — 'The Odd Women.'
'The Odd Women.'
It's comic and devastating simultaneously — the surplus women of the census, the statistical oddity, the women left over.
Gissing chose that title knowing exactly what resonance it carried — the irony is already in the very name of the thing.
That's a beautiful place to pause — the irony built into the novel's very title.
And that irony doesn't only live in the prose — it lives in the world those characters inhabit.
The grey streets, the boarding houses, the offices — the atmosphere that presses down on almost every page.
That's where we're heading next — the loneliness and atmosphere that Gissing builds around his characters, and what it tells us about the world they're trapped inside.

segments.title: Loneliness and Atmosphere: The World the Characters Inhabit

utterances.text: That ironic distance we were just tracing in Gissing's narration — it costs something, doesn't it.
Because underneath the cool observation, there's a world of quite devastating loneliness.
I want to spend some time in that world now — the physical and emotional atmosphere Gissing builds around his characters.
Caroline, you've lived with this novel for years — where do you feel that loneliness most acutely?
It's everywhere, but it's almost never announced.
Gissing doesn't say: this woman is lonely.
He puts her in a room, in a particular light, on a particular evening — and you feel it in your chest.
Think of Virginia Madden in her lodgings.
The shabbiness isn't just material poverty — it's the architecture of a life that has quietly collapsed inward.
And the way Virginia slides into her secret drinking — that's not melodrama, that's a woman who has simply run out of reasons to resist oblivion.
Gissing renders it without a word of judgment, and that restraint is what breaks you.
That architectural quality you're describing is so precise — Gissing thinks in interiors.
Every room in this novel carries a social meaning that its occupant can't quite escape.
Rhoda Nunn's rooms at Winifred's establishment are functional, deliberate — they broadcast her refusal of ornament.
But then you get Monica's domestic space after marriage to Widdowson — and it becomes a kind of elegant trap.
Gissing describes the house as comfortable, well-appointed — the language of sufficiency — and that's the horror.
Nothing is visibly wrong; everything is wrong.
There's a passage where Gissing describes Monica sitting by the window of the Herne Hill house, watching the street below.
"She was not unhappy in the sense of feeling acute misery; but a slow, dull ache possessed her, the consciousness of wasted life."
That phrase — wasted life — is almost bureaucratic in its plainness, and Gissing knows exactly what he's doing.
What strikes me is how precisely Gissing maps loneliness onto geography.
Herne Hill is a real place — it was, in the 1890s, this particular stratum of London suburbia.
Respectable, not fashionable — the kind of address that announces its occupant is trying, and has mostly succeeded, and has nothing else.
For Monica, moving there from the draper's shop is technically an ascent — and Gissing is merciless about what that ascent costs her.
She had companions at the shop, even exploited and exhausted ones.
In the Widdowson house she has comfort, isolation, and a husband who loves her in the manner of a collector who has acquired something rare and intends to keep it safe.
The historical parallel that interests me is how the Married Women's Property Acts had changed things — and yet changed so little, in practice, for women in Monica's position.
Legally, she owns herself; socially, she absolutely does not.
And Widdowson's jealousy — which Gissing traces so carefully — is almost pitiable, and yet entirely terrifying.
He follows her through London.
And Gissing gives us his point of view with such uncomfortable sympathy — we understand why he does it, which makes it worse.
There's a moment where Widdowson reflects on his own nature — that he was formed for an earlier age, when a husband's authority was unquestioned.
"He was not a bad man; he was, in truth, better than the average husband; but his temperament was that of a proprietor."
Proprietor.
That single word does everything.
It's Gissing's method in miniature, isn't it — the precision noun that closes down all escape routes.
But I keep coming back to the loneliness of the women who don't marry — which in some ways is harder to dramatise.
Monica's unhappiness has a shape — a house, a husband, a crisis.
Alice Madden's loneliness is shapeless — it's just the texture of ordinary days with no foreseeable change.
Gissing gives Alice this persistent, low-level ailment — she's always vaguely unwell — and it functions almost like a plot surrogate.
Something is always slightly wrong; nothing is ever quite crisis enough to resolve.
The Madden sisters are where the novel lives most uncomfortably, I think.
They are the "odd women" of the title in the most literal sense — numerically surplus, economically marginal.
The census data of the period is extraordinary — there really were hundreds of thousands of women in England who could not expect marriage and had no professional formation.
Gissing understood that the problem wasn't individual failure — it was structural.
Their father, Doctor Madden, is a kind and well-meaning man who has simply failed to prepare his daughters for any contingency other than a comfortable marriage.
And then he dies in the first chapter, leaving them with almost nothing.
Gissing is economical and almost brutal about it — no extended deathbed scene, no melodrama.
The catastrophe arrives, and then the novel calmly moves on — as life does, for the women left behind.
That contrast with Rhoda Nunn is what keeps the novel from being simply bleak.
Rhoda has found a purpose — Miss Barfoot's typewriting school, the whole project of making women self-sufficient.
And yet Gissing won't let her be simply heroic.
Her loneliness is different in kind — it's the loneliness of someone who has armoured herself so thoroughly that she's no longer sure what's armour and what's self.
There's a line where she says something close to: she had schooled herself to independence, but independence could be its own form of confinement.
"She had conquests enough over herself; there remained the question whether self-conquest was, in her case, the same thing as happiness."
That's the question that haunts the whole novel, for all of them.
And Gissing makes the atmosphere itself a character — the fog, the grey London light, the sensation of streets that offer no welcome.
There's a scene where Monica walks alone through the city — one of the few moments she has physical freedom — and Gissing describes the streets as indifferent.
Not hostile — indifferent.
Which is worse, in a way — hostility at least acknowledges you exist.
Gissing's London doesn't despise his women; it simply has no place for them.
And that feeling — of being uncategorised by the world — is the emotional keynote of the whole novel.
Uncategorised — and yet so precisely observed by Gissing himself.
There's a productive tension there between the warmth of the author's attention and the coldness of the world he's depicting.
All of which sets the stage rather beautifully for what comes next — because Gissing doesn't only give us bleakness.
He also gives us comedy — the absurdity of romantic misadventure, the posturing of men who are not quite equal to the women they pursue.
That's where we're headed next — the wit and folly of romance in The Odd Women.

segments.title: The Wit and Folly of Romance: Passages That Make Us Laugh and Cringe

utterances.text: We've been dwelling on the loneliness that saturates Gissing's world — the atmosphere of narrow rooms and narrower prospects.
But that same world is also, at moments, genuinely and sometimes painfully funny — especially when people try to fall in love in it.
So let's talk about the comedy of romance in The Odd Women — the scenes that make us laugh, and the ones that make us laugh while also squirming.
The first place I always go is Widdowson — Edmund Widdowson — who is one of the great comic grotesques of Victorian fiction, except that he's also terrifying.
He courts Monica with this ponderous, suffocating gravity, as if marriage were a legal instrument he needed her to sign under duress.
And the comedy is that he genuinely believes he is being romantic.
There's a moment early in their courtship where he tells Monica, in absolute earnest, that a wife's place is at her husband's side — not occasionally, but always, completely, without remainder.
And Monica listens with this surface compliance that Gissing renders with extraordinary precision — you can feel her retreating behind her own eyes.
It's both funny and horrible in exactly equal measure.
What Gissing is doing with Widdowson is something technically very intricate — he gives us free indirect discourse that slides between irony and sympathy without ever resolving.
So you're laughing at Widdowson's pomposity, but Gissing also makes sure you understand that Widdowson is sincere — he really does love Monica, in his blundering, proprietary way.
The comedy has a tragic undertow, and that tension is the engine of the whole middle section of the novel.
Gissing writes of Widdowson something like: he was not a man who could understand that a woman's nature craved more than a comfortable home and a husband's protection.
"He was not a man who could understand that a woman might wish for any life beyond the sphere he had appointed for her."
That phrase — 'appointed for her' — is doing everything: the legal register, the unconscious tyranny, the absolute confidence of the man.
And the law gave Widdowson every instrument he needed to enforce that appointment, which is what makes the comedy so uncomfortable.

Under the Married Women's Property Acts of the 1880s, Monica had gained some legal personhood — but in practice, a husband's physical and social control over his wife's movements was essentially unlimited.
Widdowson trailing Monica through the streets of London — his surveillance of her, his jealousy — that's not just psychological portrait, that's a legal reality.
The scene where he follows her and then confronts her with that wounded, righteous indignation — it's darkly farcical.
He genuinely cannot conceive that he's done anything wrong by treating his wife as a subject of surveillance.
Can we talk about Everard Barfoot for a moment, because he's a completely different species of comic disaster?
He thinks of himself as a progressive man — enlightened about women, liberated from convention — and Gissing enjoys puncturing that self-image with the subtlest possible needle.
His pursuit of Rhoda Nunn is framed, in his own mind, as an intellectual adventure — he wants to test whether a truly emancipated woman can love freely.
But what he actually wants is for Rhoda to capitulate on his terms while calling it liberation.
Gissing lets Barfoot have just enough self-awareness to be amusing, and not quite enough to be redeemed.
The great set-piece there is their debate about marriage — where Barfoot proposes what he calls a free union, without legal ceremony, as a proof of mutual trust.
And Rhoda, to her enormous credit, calls his bluff — she says, in effect, if you trust me, why does it matter whether we marry or not?
The logic is perfect and it completely wrong-foots him.
Gissing writes of Barfoot's position something to the effect that: he had imagined himself the reformer, but found that the woman he wished to reform had a clearer head than his own.
"It irritated him that she should be so clear of brain when he was struggling with emotions he had thought himself superior to."
The irony lands so quietly — 'thought himself superior to' — and the whole masculine project of his courtship collapses in that phrase.
Barfoot is a recognisable type from the 1890s — the New Man who discovers, when actually confronted with a New Woman, that his progressivism was largely theoretical.
There were real debates in feminist and socialist circles at the time about free unions — Edward Carpenter was writing about this, various Fabian households were experimenting.
And the consistent finding, if I can call it that, was that men tended to benefit more from the arrangement than women — rather as Rhoda suspects.
Gissing was absolutely on to something that his contemporaries were living through in real time.
And then there's poor Virginia Madden — who I find the most quietly heartbreaking comic figure in the whole novel.
Her romance — if you can call it that — with sherry is handled with this devastating deadpan that Gissing rarely deploys quite so mercilessly.
She begins drinking to dull the loneliness we were just discussing, and then the drinking becomes its own companionship.

There's a scene where she prepares herself for an outing and Gissing describes her flushed cheeks and slightly elevated spirits with a clinical neutrality that is somehow more wounding than explicit condemnation.
You want to laugh — the picture is almost farcical — and then you realise you're watching a woman disappear.
That neutrality is the key to Gissing's comic register throughout the novel — he very rarely tips into satire, because satire requires a stable moral position from which to mock.
Gissing is too pessimistic — or too honest, depending on how you read him — to stand anywhere that securely.
So his comedy is always embedded in sympathy — even Widdowson gets his moment of genuine pathos.
That's what makes it cringe rather than simply funny — you're never fully permitted the distance of pure ridicule.
I think the funniest and most cringeworthy exchange in the novel is actually between Monica and Widdowson on the subject of her going out to shop alone.
He has objections — grave, considered, deeply felt objections — to her making independent excursions into London.
And he presents these objections with the full weight of his authority, never apparently sensing how grotesque they sound.
Gissing gives Widdowson lines that are almost self-parodying — something very close to: he could not bear to think of her in the streets unprotected, subjected to the gaze of strangers.
"It was not distrust of her — he wished her to understand that — but the world was full of dangers for a woman so young and so attractive."
The hedging — 'it was not distrust of her' — is magnificent, because of course it absolutely is distrust of her.
And Monica says almost nothing in return — which is its own kind of comedy.
Her silences are so loaded throughout the novel — Gissing uses them structurally, as places where the reader has to do the work.
We fill in what she's thinking, and what we fill in is usually bleak and funny at once.
What strikes me listening to all of this is that Gissing uses comedy as a kind of pressure gauge — the more absurd the romantic situation, the higher the pressure underneath it.
And those pressures — of principle, of compromise, of what you give up and what you hold on to — are exactly where we're heading next.

segments.title: What Remains: Principle, Compromise, and the Cost of Choice

utterances.text: We've been laughing at Gissing's wit — and sometimes wincing at it — but underneath all that irony runs something far more serious.
This final stretch of the novel is really about what it costs to hold a principle — or to abandon one.
And I think the novel's deepest structural gamble is precisely that Gissing refuses to let principle be painless.
Rhoda Nunn is the figure who carries that weight most visibly — she has built her entire identity on the rejection of romantic compromise.
And yet when Everard Barfoot enters her life, Gissing doesn't let her off the hook easily.
He makes her feel — genuinely feel — and then he uses that feeling as an argument against everything she stands for.
The craft move I keep returning to is how Gissing withholds Rhoda's interior at the most dramatic moments — we see her position but not her full anguish.
That reticence is doing enormous narrative work.
I'd put it in slightly harder historical terms: what Rhoda is defending isn't just a philosophy — it's a practical survival strategy for women of her class and time.
The whole apparatus of the Widdowson marriage — that locked drawing-room world — shows what matrimony actually meant legally and socially in the 1890s.
A wife had almost no independent legal standing.
Gissing makes Edmund Widdowson a man who genuinely believes he loves Monica — which is almost the most frightening thing about him.
His tyranny doesn't come from malice; it comes from the marriage law internalised as natural feeling.
Monica pays for that with her life, and the novel is absolutely clear-eyed about it.
Monica's death always stops me cold, every time I read it.
She dies having made what felt like a choice — leaving Widdowson, pursuing something beyond him — and yet she is utterly destroyed by the consequences.
There's a line late in the novel where Gissing describes Rhoda looking at the infant Monica has left behind, and Rhoda has what I can only call a moment of reckoning.
Gissing writes that the child was "unconscious of its loss" — those four words carry the whole weight of the novel's bleakness.
The innocent cannot even register what has been taken from them.
And that bleakness falls on Rhoda, who has survived — which is its own kind of verdict.
That word 'survived' is exactly right — and Gissing refuses to make survival triumphant.
The final image of Rhoda is not victory; it's endurance.
She holds to her work, her mission, the school for women's independence — but Everard has gone off and married someone entirely conventional.
That's the novel's sharpest irony: the man who claimed to admire female independence chooses, in the end, the path of least resistance.
Gissing doesn't editorialize — he simply shows it and lets the juxtaposition do the work.
Everard is a fascinating case because he thinks of himself as progressive — and in some technical sense he is, compared to Widdowson.
But his progressivism is entirely self-serving — it flatters him to admire Rhoda's independence until it demands something of him.
He proposes what amounts to a trial marriage — cohabitation without legal sanction — which he frames as radical honesty.
In practice, of course, the risk falls almost entirely on Rhoda — socially, professionally, personally.
Gissing was writing in the 1890s, but that particular dynamic has a remarkably long shelf life.
What I find most moving — and most true — is that Rhoda doesn't entirely escape wanting what she's renounced.
There's real grief in her when Everard finally goes — Gissing doesn't pretend her principles inoculate her against loss.
Mary Barfoot says something to her — I'm paraphrasing — to the effect that the work must be enough.
And Rhoda receives that — holds it — but Gissing leaves us uncertain whether she believes it.
That uncertainty is where the novel's emotional honesty lives.
And that's what separates Gissing from so many of his contemporaries writing about the New Woman.
He doesn't give us a heroine whose convictions are cost-free, and he doesn't punish her for having them either.
The title itself — 'The Odd Women' — gestures toward all the women who didn't fit the expected narrative.
Odd in the statistical sense — surplus to the marriage market — but also odd in the sense of eccentric, resistant, irreducible.
Gissing honors that irreducibility even when he cannot offer it a happy ending.
The Madden sisters are the undersung tragedy of this book, I always think.
They represent the women who received no education, no preparation, no framework for thinking about their own lives differently.
Virginia's decline into alcoholism, Alice's grinding genteel poverty — these are not melodrama.
They are the statistical reality of what happened to middle-class women without capital or skills in late Victorian England.
Rhoda and Mary Barfoot are trying, with inadequate resources, to prevent the next generation of Madden sisters.
The stakes of their project are embodied in those three women — that's the real argument of the novel.
I come back to the novel every few years and I find different things each time.
When I was younger I was entirely on Rhoda's side — her refusals felt heroic.
Now I feel more of the cost alongside the heroism — which I think is exactly what Gissing intended.
The novel grows with you.
That might be the finest thing you can say about any novel — that it grows with you.
What we've traced across this episode is a book that refuses easy consolations at every turn.
The comedy of manners that makes us laugh, the structural choices that make us admire, and the human cost that makes us grieve.
My warmest thanks to Dr. Eleanor Hartley, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — this has been a genuinely illuminating conversation.
And to our listeners — thank you for spending this time with Gissing and with us.
The Odd Women rewards every hour you give it.
